summary: Victor Savkin opens with an extended metaphor: a genie materializes John Carmack in his prime to help your codebase, but with two crippling restrictions—he can only see 1/1000 of the code and remembers nothing between sessions. This is what coding agents are today. A concrete example: changing a UI library and propagating it through four repos requires seven separate explanations for one change, because each interaction starts with a fresh, context-free agent. Savkin identifies two root problem categories. The space component: agents are repo-bound, seeing one repo at a time, never the whole system. The time component: agents have no episodic memory—every session is blank, and the human becomes the memory. To solve this, Nx built Polygraph, an agent-agnostic meta-harness. It analyzes thousands of repos accessible to a GitHub user, extracts metadata (what each repo produces, consumes, APIs, package dependencies), and stitches them into a unified dependency graph. Polygraph sets up multi-repo sessions with per-repo agents, treats multi-repo CI as one vector, and captures all agent traces, intent, PRs, and repo involvement to restore episodic memory. The demo shows creating a session by selecting repos, picking an agent (Claude), and having the agent plan and implement changes across both repos as if in a single repo. A second demo shows resuming the session on a different machine with a different agent (Cortex), reconstructing the same repos, SHAs, and setup, with the agent primed from the captured trace. Savkin likens this to a Star Trek transporter—full session state materialized on another machine, enabling zero-setup PR review by resuming a coworker's session. He demonstrates a bug-fix flow where simply telling the agent a session is broken causes it to download relevant repos, shards, and logs to reconstruct state and produce a fix. Beyond manual repo selection, the graph's intelligence enables natural-language queries like finding every repo depending on a library version, or discovering past sessions relevant to new work—promoting cross-repo consistency by replicating approaches from respected engineers. Polygraph can also be invoked from within an existing agent session to add repos mid-work, which Savkin prefers over tools like context seven because having the real code lets agents go deep. He closes with a Borg-like hive mind vision: across a thousand engineers, every session and decision is accessible to every agent, giving any single agent more context than any single developer.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The Genius with Amnesia Metaphor
sections.summary: Savkin introduces a genie metaphor: John Carmack in his prime is granted to help your project, but can only see 1/1000 of the codebase and remembers nothing between interactions. This genius-with-amnesia scenario is what coding agents are today.

sections.title: The Re-explanation Problem
sections.summary: A concrete example of changing a UI library and propagating through four repos (UI, module one, module two, platform) requires seven separate explanations for one change, because each interaction starts with a fresh agent lacking context.

sections.title: Two Categories of Agent Limitations
sections.summary: Two root problems: agents are repo-bound (space component)—they see one repo at a time, cannot align changes, reference cross-repo standards, validate downstream, or update consumers. And agents forget (time component)—no episodic memory, human becomes the memory.

sections.title: The Graph of Work vs What Agents See
sections.summary: The real graph of organizational work has a repository graph at the bottom (artifacts plus open source deps) and session graph at top, with relationships between repos and sessions. The agent sees only one session and one small fraction with no memory.

sections.title: Introducing Polygraph and Unified Dependency Graph
sections.summary: Nx built Polygraph, an agent-agnostic meta-harness. It analyzes thousands of repos a GitHub user can access, extracts metadata (produces, consumes, APIs, package dependencies), and stitches them into a unified dependency graph creating the illusion of one big codebase.

sections.title: Multi-repo Sessions, CI Coordination, and Episodic Memory
sections.summary: Polygraph sets up multi-repo sessions with per-repo agents, treats all CI as one vector (determining which repo needs fixing on failure), and captures agent traces, intent, PRs, and repo involvement to restore episodic memory—yielding an agent with photographic memory of the organization.

sections.title: Demo: Creating and Resuming Sessions
sections.summary: Demo shows creating a session by selecting backend and frontend repos, picking Claude as agent, and the agent planning and implementing changes across both repos as if single-repo. A second demo shows resuming the session on a different machine with a different agent (Cortex), reconstructing the same repos, SHAs, and setup, primed with the captured trace.

sections.title: Session Resumption, PR Review, and Agent Switching
sections.summary: Savkin likens session resumption to a Star Trek transporter—full session state materialized on another machine. He uses this for PR review: instead of asking the author questions, he resumes their session with zero setup and queries his own agent about decisions, since all traces are captured. He notes this also enables switching agents mid-session, e.g., from Claude to Codex when something goes down.

sections.title: Bug Fix via Session Reference
sections.summary: Demo of referencing a broken production session: the user simply tells the agent the session is broken, and the agent downloads relevant repos, shards, and agent logs from the original session to reconstruct state and produce a fix—no extra information required from the user.

sections.title: Graph-Driven Repo and Session Discovery
sections.summary: Instead of manually selecting repos, users can ask the agent in natural language to find every repo depending on a particular library version and update it. The graph's intelligence also supports loose queries—finding relevant sessions for a blog post or new feature like adding a vector index, promoting cross-repo consistency by replicating approaches from respected engineers' sessions.

sections.title: Repo-Session Intelligence and Mid-Session Repo Addition
sections.summary: Polygraph prioritizes sessions relevant to a repo and vice versa. Beyond the CLI, Polygraph can be invoked from within an existing agent session to add repos mid-work—e.g., adding the Vitest open-source repo to an Nx session. Savkin prefers this over context seven because having real code lets agents discover deep problems.

sections.title: Conclusion: Lifting Space and Time Constraints
sections.summary: Savkin recapitulates: agents are constrained in space and time, but Polygraph lifts both—giving agents access to all reachable code (owned and open source) and a perfect memory of every session and decision. With a thousand engineers, every agent contributes to a shared hive mind, giving any single agent more context than any single developer. He directs listeners to try.poligraph.com.

demonstrations: Creating a Polygraph session: selecting backend and frontend repos, naming the session, picking Claude as agent, agent plans and implements changes across both repos as if in a single repo
Resuming a session on a different machine: coworker receives session, uses different agent (Cortex), same repos and SHAs reconstructed, agent primed with captured trace from original session
Bug fix by referencing a session: user says a session is broken, agent downloads relevant repos, shards, and logs, reconstructs state, and produces the fix with no extra information from the user
Auto-selecting repos via graph queries: telling the agent to find every repo depending on a particular library version and update them, without manual selection
Finding relevant past sessions for new work: searching for sessions relevant to adding a vector index into the PR collection, loading them for best practices and consistency
Adding repos mid-session from within an existing agent: working in a Claude session on an Nx repo, asking to add the Vitest open-source repo so the agent can explore real code and resolve issues
limitations: Agents are repo-bound, seeing one repo at a time
Agents have no episodic memory, every session starts blank
Agents cannot update consumers while making source changes
Agents cannot reference best practices and standards in other repos
Without Polygraph, every cross-repo implementation is bespoke with no consistency
